title: Threat-model the file upload path and fix findings
prompt: Threat-model the file upload path and fix findings

steps.text: File upload is one of the most attacked surfaces in any app. I will walk the data flow from the browser to storage and back to the download link, apply STRIDE at each trust boundary, and then fix what the walk finds, with a test per fix. Typical suspects: trusting the client content type, path traversal in the stored name, unbounded size, no malware scan, and download links that never expire.
I'll threat-model the upload path with STRIDE across its trust boundaries, then fix every finding rated medium or above, each with a regression test. Reading the upload code.

steps.content:
# Threat model: file upload

Data flow: browser -> API (/files) -> local disk -> /files/:name download.
Trust boundaries: TB1 internet to API, TB2 API to storage, TB3 storage to other users' browsers.

| ID | STRIDE | Boundary | Finding | Rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UP-1 | Tampering | TB2 | `file.name` joined into the path: traversal (`../../etc/cron.d/x`) | High |
| UP-2 | Denial of service | TB1 | No size limit on the multipart body | High |
| UP-3 | Spoofing | TB3 | Client-supplied content type served back: stored XSS via `text/html` | High |
| UP-4 | Elevation | TB2 | No malware scan before files are shared | Medium |
| UP-5 | Information disclosure | TB3 | Download URLs are guessable and never expire | Medium |
| UP-6 | Repudiation | TB1 | Uploads are not audited | Low |

steps.text: Six findings: three high (path traversal, no size limit, stored XSS via the client content type), two medium, one low. Fixing all six. A subagent will build the malicious-file test corpus in parallel.

steps.context: Repo: sample-platform. Threat model docs/threat-models/file-upload.md lists UP-1..UP-6. Fixes go in src/files/*. Tests in tests/files/.

tasks.name: UploadAttackCorpus
tasks.task: Build a test corpus of hostile uploads covering UP-1 to UP-6: traversal names, oversized bodies, polyglot HTML/image files, the EICAR test string, double extensions and null bytes, and a test that runs each through the upload route.
tasks.result:
# UploadAttackCorpus

tests/files/corpus/: 18 hostile samples (traversal x4, polyglots x3, double extensions x3, null byte names x2, EICAR x1, oversized x2, svg with script x3). tests/files/hostile.test.ts runs each through POST /files and asserts refusal or safe storage.

steps.text: Polyglots matter most: a valid PNG header followed by HTML defeats naive magic-byte checks unless the server also forces the served type.
18 hostile samples and a table-driven test over all of them.

steps.text: The storage layer must not let a caller pick the key prefix, otherwise UP-1 comes back through the storage API instead of the file system. Checking its config before running the tests.

steps.text:
Threat model done and every finding fixed:

| ID | Finding | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| UP-1 | Path traversal via file name | Server-chosen ids; client name is metadata only |
| UP-2 | No size limit | 25 MB cap checked before and after parsing |
| UP-3 | Stored XSS via client content type | Magic-byte sniffing, allowlist, attachment + nosniff |
| UP-4 | No malware scan | Scan before storage, infected files quarantined |
| UP-5 | Guessable, permanent links | HMAC-signed, user-bound, 10 minute expiry |
| UP-6 | No audit | Upload audit events |

9/9 tests including an 18-sample hostile corpus; SAST and DAST clean. The model lives in `docs/threat-models/file-upload.md`.
